title: International Union, UAW v. Brock
summary: A union could challenge a common federal interpretation restricting workers’ readjustment benefits while individual eligibility determinations remained with state authorities.
notes: The vote was 5-4: Justice Marshall wrote for the Court, reversing and remanding; Justice White dissented joined by Chief Justice Burger and Justice Rehnquist, and Justice Powell filed a separate dissent. The benefits were trade readjustment allowances under the Trade Act of 1974 and the challenged interpretation was the Secretary of Labor's 1975 guidelines; the D.C. Circuit had relied on 19 U.S.C. § 2311(d) to require joinder of the state agencies.

sections.Parties: The United Auto Workers and individual members challenged a Department of Labor guideline administered under the Trade Act of 1974. The Secretary of Labor defended the guideline and opposed the union’s ability to litigate for members.
sections.Material Facts: The program provided federally funded readjustment allowances to workers displaced by import competition. The challengers contended that the Department’s eligibility interpretation unlawfully restricted benefits. Many union members had been denied allowances because of the federal interpretation, and some still had live claims. The union sought a ruling on the governing interpretation, leaving state authorities to decide each claimant’s eligibility and benefits.
sections.Procedural History: The district court granted relief on the legal interpretation. The court of appeals held that individual members could not proceed without joining state agencies and that the union lacked standing. The Supreme Court reversed those rulings. The assigned discussion concentrates on the union’s standing and the nature of the relief, rather than supplying the entire substantive benefit dispute.
sections.Issue: Whether the union satisfied the three-part associational-standing test when individual members’ ultimate benefit awards could differ but the federal suit addressed a common legal interpretation.
sections.Holding: The union could sue on behalf of affected members. At least some members had live standing, the challenge was germane to the union’s purpose, and the legal claim and requested remedy did not require every member’s individual participation. The ruling did not itself award every member benefits.
sections.Reasoning: The Court distinguished a challenge to the Secretary’s legal directive from a direct federal adjudication of individual state benefit determinations. Because the former was the actual claim, state review rules and unresolved individual amounts did not defeat the suit. The union’s constitution and advocacy showed that unemployment-related benefits were germane to its purposes. Unlike the member-specific damages claim discussed in Warth, the requested ruling presented a common legal question and reserved individual applications for the designated authorities. The Court also emphasized the expertise, resources, and preexisting representative relationship an association can provide. It acknowledged possible inadequate representation or member conflicts but found no reason on this record to abandon established associational standing. A judgment’s effect on absent members could separately raise due-process questions if representation were deficient.

topics.lrs-n-standing-association: Brock applies each Hunt requirement to a common legal question with individual benefit proceedings left intact.
topics.lrs-n-standing-third-party: White's dissent attacked Hunt-style associational standing as a form of third-party litigation, so the case frames the association/third-party boundary.
